19 if he rises again and walks around with his staff, then he who struck him shall be cleared; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall provide for his healing until he is thoroughly healed. 20 “If a man⌘ strikes his servant or his maid with a rod, and he dies under his hand, the man shall surely be punished. 21 Notwithstanding, if his servant gets up after a day or two, he shall not be punished, for the servant is his property. 22 “If men fight and hurt a pregnant woman⌘ so that she gives birth prematurely, and yet no harm follows, he shall be surely fined as much as the woman’s husband demands and the judges allow. 23 But if any harm follows, then you must take life for life, 24 eye for eye, tooth for tooth◇, hand for hand, foot for foot, 25 burning for burning, wound for wound, and bruise for bruise. 26 “If a man⌘ strikes his servant’s eye, or his maid’s eye, and destroys it, he shall let him go free for his eye’s sake. 27 If he strikes out his male servant’s tooth, or his female servant’s tooth, he shall let the servant go free for his tooth’s sake. 28 “If a bull gores a man⌘ or a woman⌘ to death, the bull shall surely be stoned, and its meat shall not be eaten; but the owner of the bull shall not be held responsible. 29 But if the bull had a habit of goring in the past, and this has been testified to its owner, and he has not kept it in, but it has killed a man⌘ or a woman⌘, the bull shall be stoned, and its owner shall also be put to death. 30 If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed. 31 Whether it has gored a son or has gored a daughter, according to this judgment it shall be done to him. 32 If the bull gores a male servant or a female servant, thirty shekels of silver shall be given to their master, and the ox shall be stoned. 33 “If a man⌘ opens a pit, or if a man digs a pit and doesn’t cover it, and a bull or a donkey falls into it, 34 the owner of the pit shall make it good⌘. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead animal shall be his. 35 “If one man⌘’s bull injures another’s, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live bull, and divide its price; and they shall also divide the dead animal. 36 Or if it is known that the bull was in the habit of goring in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall surely pay bull for bull, and the dead animal shall be his own.

22

1 “If a man⌘ steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall pay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep. 2 If the thief is found breaking in, and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no guilt of blood⌘shed for him. 3 If the sun has risen on him, he is guilty of blood⌘shed. He shall make restitution. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft. 4 If the stolen property is found in his hand alive, whether it is ox, donkey, or sheep, he shall pay double. 5 “If a man⌘ causes a field or vineyard to be eaten by letting his animal loose, and it grazes in another man’s field, he shall make restitution from the best of his own field, and from the best of his own vineyard. 6 “If fire breaks out, and catches in thorns so that the shocks of grain, or the standing grain, or the field are consumed; he who kindled the fire shall surely make restitution. 7 “If a man⌘ delivers to his neighbor money or stuff to keep, and it is stolen out of the man’s house, if the thief is found, he shall pay double. 8 If the thief isn’t found, then the master of the house shall come near to God, to find out whether or not he has put his hand on his neighbor’s goods. 9 For every matter of trespass, whether it is for ox, for donkey, for sheep, for clothing, or for any kind of lost thing, about which one says, ‘This is mine,’ the cause of both parties shall come before God. He whom God condemns shall pay double to his neighbor. 10 “If a man⌘ delivers to his neighbor a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured, or driven away, no man seeing it; 11 the oath of Yahweh shall be between them both, he has not put his hand on his neighbor’s good⌘s; and its owner shall accept it, and he shall not make restitution. 12 But if it is stolen from him, the one who stole shall make restitution to its owner. 13 If it is torn in pieces, let him bring it for evidence. He shall not make good⌘ that which was torn. 14 “If a man⌘ borrows anything of his neighbor’s, and it is injured, or dies, its owner not being with it, he shall surely make restitution. 15 If its owner is with it, he shall not make it good⌘. If it is a leased thing, it came for its lease. 16 “If a man⌘ entices a virgin who isn’t pledged to be married, and lies with her, he shall surely pay a dowry for her to be his wife. 17 If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins. 18 “You shall not allow a sorceress to live.‖ 19 “Whoever has sex with an animal shall surely be put to death. 20 “He who sacrifices to any god⌘, except to Yahweh only, shall be utterly destroyed. 21 “You shall not wrong an alien◇ or oppress him, for you were aliens in the land⌘ of Egypt. 22 “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. 23 If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry; 24 and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless. 25 “If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be to him as a creditor. You shall not charge him interest. 26 If you take your neighbor’s garment as collateral, you shall restore it to him before the sun goes down, 27 for that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. What would he sleep in? It will happen, when he cries to me, that I will hear, for I am gracious. 28 “You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler◇ of your people. 29 “You shall not delay to offer from your harvest and from the outflow of your presses. “You shall give the firstborn of your sons to me. 30 You shall do likewise with your cattle and with your sheep. It shall be with its mother seven days, then on the eighth day you shall give it to me. 31 “You shall be holy⌘ men to me, therefore you shall not eat any meat that is torn by animals in the field. You shall cast it to the dogs.

23

1 “You shall not spread a false report. Don’t join your hand with the wicked to be a malicious witness. 2 “You shall not follow a crowd to do evil. You shall not testify in court to side with a multitude to pervert justice. 3 You shall not favor a poor man⌘ in his cause. 4 “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. 5 If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him. You shall surely help him with it. 6 “You shall not deny justice to your poor people in their lawsuits. 7 “Keep far from a false charge, and don’t kill the innocent and righteous⌘; for I will not justify the wicked. 8 “You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds those who have sight and perverts the words of the righteous⌘. 9 “You shall not oppress an alien◇, for you know the heart⌘ of an alien, since you were aliens in the land⌘ of Egypt. 10 “For six years you shall sow your land⌘, and shall gather in its increase, 11 but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the animal of the field shall eat. In the same way, you shall deal with your vineyard and with your olive grove. 12 “Six days you shall do your work, and on the seventh day you shall rest, that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant, and the alien may be refreshed. 13 “Be careful to do all things that I have said to you; and don’t invoke the name of other gods or even let them be heard out of your mouth. 14 “You shall observe a feast to me three times a year. 15 You shall observe the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib (for in it you came out of Egypt), and no one shall appear before me empty⌘. 16 And the feast of harvest, the first fruits of your labors, which you sow in the field; and the feast of ingathering, at the end of the year, when you gather in your labors out of the field. 17 Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord⌘ Yahweh. 18 “You shall not offer the blood⌘ of my sacrifice with leavened bread. The fat of my feast shall not remain all night until the morning. 19 You shall bring the first of the first fruits of your ground into the house of Yahweh your God⌘. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk◇. 20 “Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you by the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.‖‖ 21 Pay attention to him, and listen to his voice. Don’t provoke him, for he will not pardon your disobedience, for my name is in him. 22 But if you indeed listen to his voice, and do all that I speak, then I will be an enemy to your enemies, and an adversary to your adversaries.‖ 23 For my angel shall go before you, and bring you in to the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; and I will cut them off. 24 You shall not bow down to their gods, nor serve them, nor follow their practices, but you shall utterly overthrow them and demolish their pillars. 25 You shall serve Yahweh your God⌘, and he will bless your bread and your water⌘, and I will take sickness away from among you.‖‖ 26 No one will miscarry or be barren in your land⌘. I will fulfill the number of your days.‖ 27 I will send my terror before you, and will confuse all the people to whom you come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.‖ 28 I will send the hornet before you, which will drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite, from before you. 29 I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land⌘ become desolate, and the animals of the field multiply against you. 30 Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and inherit the land⌘. 31 I will set your border from the Red Sea even to the sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River; for I will deliver the inhabitants of the land⌘ into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you. 32 You shall make no covenant⌘ with them, nor with their gods. 33 They shall not dwell in your land⌘, lest they make you sin⌘ against me, for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.”

24

1 He said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance. 2 Moses alone shall come near to Yahweh, but they shall not come near. The people shall not go up with him.” 3 Moses came and told the people all Yahweh’s words, and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, “All the words which Yahweh has spoken will we do.” 4 Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, then rose up early in the morning and built an altar at the base of the mountain, with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. 5 He sent young men of the children of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace⌘ offerings of cattle to Yahweh. 6 Moses took half of the blood⌘ and put it in basins, and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar.‖ 7 He took the book of the covenant⌘ and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “We will do all that Yahweh has said, and be obedient.” 8 Moses took the blood⌘, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant⌘◇, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”‖◇ 9 Then Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up. 10 They saw the God⌘ of Israel◇. Under his feet was like a paved work of sapphire stone, like the skies for clearness. 11 He didn’t lay his hand on the nobles of the children of Israel. They saw God⌘, and ate and drank. 12 Yahweh said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain, and stay here, and I will give you the stone tablets with the law and the commands that I have written, that you may teach them.” 13 Moses rose up with Joshua, his servant, and Moses went up onto God⌘’s Mountain. 14 He said to the elders, “Wait here for us, until we come again to you. Behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever is involved in a dispute can go to them.” 15 Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. 16 Yahweh’s glory⌘ settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the middle of the cloud. 17 The appearance of Yahweh’s glory⌘ was like devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the eyes of the children of Israel. 18 Moses entered into the middle of the cloud, and went up on the mountain; and Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

25

1 2 Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel, that they take an offering for me. From everyone whose heart⌘ makes him willing you shall take my offering. 3 This is the offering which you shall take from them: gold, silver, bronze, 4 blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, 5 rams’ skins dyed red, sea cow hides, acacia wood, 6 oil for the light⌘, spices for the anointing oil and for the sweet incense, 7 onyx stones, and stones to be set for the ephod and for the breastplate. 8 Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them⌘⌘.‖◇ 9 According to all that I show you, the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all of its furniture, even so you shall make it. 10 “They shall make an ark of acacia wood. Its length shall be two and a half cubits, its width a cubit and a half, and a cubit and a half its height. 11 You shall overlay it with pure gold. You shall overlay it inside and outside, and you shall make a gold molding around it. 12 You shall cast four rings of gold for it, and put them in its four feet. Two rings shall be on the one side of it, and two rings on the other side of it. 13 You shall make poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold. 14 You shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark. 15 The poles shall be in the rings of the ark. They shall not be taken from it. 16 You shall put the covenant which I shall give you into the ark. 17 You shall make a mercy⌘ seat of pure gold. Two and a half cubits shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its width. 18 You shall make two cherubim of hammered gold. You shall make them at the two ends of the mercy⌘ seat.◇ 19 Make one cherub at the one end, and one cherub at the other end. You shall make the cherubim on its two ends of one piece with the mercy⌘ seat. 20 The cherubim shall spread out their wings upward, covering the mercy⌘ seat with their wings, with their faces toward one another. The faces of the cherubim shall be toward the mercy seat. 21 You shall put the mercy⌘ seat on top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the covenant that I will give you. 22 There I will meet with you, and I will tell you from above the mercy⌘ seat, from between the two cherubim which are on the ark of the covenant, all that I command you for the children of Israel. 23 “You shall make a table of acacia wood. Its length shall be two cubits, and its width a cubit, and its height one and a half cubits. 24 You shall overlay it with pure gold, and make a gold molding around it. 25 You shall make a rim of a hand width around it. You shall make a golden molding on its rim around it. 26 You shall make four rings of gold for it, and put the rings in the four corners that are on its four feet. 27 The rings shall be close to the rim, for places for the poles to carry the table. 28 You shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold, that the table may be carried with them. 29 You shall make its dishes, its spoons, its ladles, and its bowls with which to pour out offerings. You shall make them of pure gold. 30 You shall set bread of the presence on the table before me always. 31 “You shall make a lamp stand of pure gold. The lamp stand shall be made of hammered work. Its base, its shaft, its cups, its buds, and its flowers shall be of one piece with it. 32 There shall be six branches going out of its sides: three branches of the lamp stand out of its one side, and three branches of the lamp stand out of its other side; 33 three cups made like almond blossoms in one branch, a bud and a flower; and three cups made like almond blossoms in the other branch, a bud and a flower, so for the six branches going out of the lamp stand; 34 and in the lamp stand four cups made like almond blossoms, its buds and its flowers; 35 and a bud under two branches of one piece with it, and a bud under two branches of one piece with it, and a bud under two branches of one piece with it, for the six branches going out of the lamp stand. 36 Their buds and their branches shall be of one piece with it, all of it one beaten work of pure gold. 37 You shall make its lamps seven, and they shall light⌘ its lamps to give light to the space in front of it. 38 Its snuffers and its snuff dishes shall be of pure gold. 39 It shall be made of a talent of pure gold, with all these accessories. 40 See that you make them after their pattern, which has been shown to you on the mountain.

Notes

◇ Note. Bridge to Genesis. The opening words in Hebrew (v’elleh shemot, “and these are the names”) begin with the conjunction and, deliberately stitching Exodus to the closing of Genesis. The Hebrew title of the book, Shemot (“Names”), comes from this first phrase; the English title Exodus follows the LXX Éxodos (“departure / way out”).

⌘ Hebrew. Sharatz (שָׁרַץ) — “swarmed.” The same verb appears in Genesis 1:20–21 of fish and creeping things multiplying. Its application to humans here is unusual and faintly unsettling: Israel’s growth is described in the language of a teeming animal population, foreshadowing why the Egyptians will fear them. The cluster of five fertility verbs in this verse (were fruitful, increased, multiplied, grew strong, filled) deliberately echoes the creation blessing of Genesis 1:28.

⌘ Word. Pithom and Pi-Ramesses. Pi-Ramesses (modern Qantir) was the Nile-delta capital built under Ramesses II in the 13th century BCE; Pithom (Per-Atum) sat nearby. Their naming is one of the few Exodus details with direct archaeological tie-ins, and is a key data-point in debates over the date of the exodus (a 13th-century date fits these names; a 15th-century date would require the names to be later editorial updates).

⌘ Hebrew. Shiphrah (שִׁפְרָה) and Puah (פּוּעָה). The names mean roughly “Beauty” and “Splendor” / “Fragrance.” The narrative names two midwives but never names the Pharaoh — a quiet inversion of imperial power. Whether the two were Hebrew women or Egyptian women serving Hebrews is grammatically ambiguous in the Hebrew (m’yalledot ha-‘Ivriyyot can be read either way); ancient and modern interpreters split.

⌘ Hebrew. Chayot (חָיוֹת) — “lively.” The midwives’ excuse plays on a word that elsewhere means simply “animals.” Their report flatters the Egyptian stereotype of Hebrews as a lower-status, more bestial people, and the king accepts it. Rabbinic tradition (b. Sotah 11b) reads the line ironically — the midwives are gently mocking Pharaoh.

⌘ Hebrew. Tevah (תֵּבָה) — “ark.” The Hebrew word here is the same one used for Noah’s ark in Genesis 6–9, and appears in only these two contexts in the entire Hebrew Bible. The lexical link is deliberate: a small floating box carries the rescuer through hostile waters, just as the great floating box once carried the seed of humanity. In each case God preserves life through pitch-sealed wood.

⌘ Hebrew. Mosheh (מֹשֶׁה) — Moses. The Hebrew etymology supplied by the text (meshitihu, “I drew him out”) is a folk-pun: grammatically the name is active (“one who draws out”), not passive (“drawn out”). Linguistically the name is almost certainly Egyptian — the same element seen in Thutmose, Ahmose, Ramesses (Egyptian ms / mes, “born of / son”). Pharaoh’s daughter would naturally have given an Egyptian name; the Hebrew text re-reads it as prophecy of his future role.

⌘ Hebrew. Tza‘aqah (צְעָקָה) — “outcry.” The same noun used for Sodom’s cry (Gen 18:20–21) and the cry of the oppressed throughout the Hebrew Bible. It triggers the four-verb sequence that follows in 2:24–25 — God heard, remembered, saw, knew — each rendered active and concrete. In Hebrew idiom, divine “remembering” (zakhar) is never mental recall but always the prelude to intervention; the cry inaugurates the liberation that the rest of the book unfolds.

⌘ Hebrew. ʼĕlôhîym (אֱלֹהִים). gods in the ordinary sense; but specifically used (in the plural thus, especially with the article) of the supreme God; occasionally applied by way of deference to magistrates; and sometimes as a superlative. [Reviewer: extend this with context, theological reading, and any cross-canon resonance before promoting.]

⌘ Hebrew. S’neh (סְנֶה) — “bramble.” The unusual word for the burning shrub (used in only two passages of the Bible, both Mosaic) is widely thought to pun on Sinai (Sinai / S’neh) — the mountain of revelation embedded already in the bush of revelation. Rabbinic tradition asks why God appears in a thornbush and not a great cedar; one answer (Shemot Rabbah 2:5) is that no place is too low for the divine presence.

‖ Cite. Cross-references. Act 7:30. [Reviewer: select 1–3 most relevant; rewrite as a thematic note rather than a list before promoting.]

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Nativity (c. 365 AD)

The bush that burns yet is not consumed is, for Ephrem, the first canonical type of the Theotokos: the holy fire of divinity dwelling within the bush of Mary's flesh without consuming it. Tewahedo iconography seats the burning bush among its earliest Marian types, and the bush is a regular figure in Marian hymnody: 'the bush that bore the fire and was not burned.'

◇ Note. Removing sandals. Footwear removal as a sign of stepping onto sacred space is well-attested across the ancient Near East and survives in Islamic and many Eastern Christian practice today. Joshua receives the same instruction at Jericho (Josh 5:15). The leather of the sandal — once an animal — is what is excluded, perhaps marking the boundary between mortal flesh and divine ground.

⌘ Hebrew. Ehyeh asher Ehyeh (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה). Famously untranslatable. The Hebrew imperfect ehyeh can mean “I am,” “I will be,” or “I am becoming.” Possible readings: (1) absolute declaration of being (the philosophical reading, picked up by the LXX egō eimi ho ōn, “I am the One who is”); (2) a refusal to be pinned down — “I will be whatever I will be”; (3) a covenantal promise — “I will be present [for you].” The construction also stands deliberately close to the divine name YHWH (3rd-person of the same root) given in the next verse.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (363). Ephrem the Syrian Sermo de Domino Nostro (c. 363 AD)

'I AM THAT I AM' is, for Ephrem, the divine Name revealed in advance of the Incarnation as the very ground on which the Word may later say 'Before Abraham was, I am' (Jn 8:58). The Name is not given to Moses as a label but as a confession: God reveals himself as the eternal subsisting One whose being underwrites every act of deliverance. Tewahedo reads Ex 3:14 and Jn 8:58 as a single canonical disclosure.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria De Decretis Nicaenae Synodi §22 (c. 350 AD)

'And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM... Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you' — Athanasius marks the LXX egō eimi ho ōn (I-AM the-Being-One) as the foundational name-of-God revelation that the Word inherits and reveals in Jn 8:58 (prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi — 'before Abraham was, I am'). The divine egō-eimi is unshareable with any creature; that the incarnate-Word uses it self-referentially at Jn 6:35 + 8:12 + 10:7 + 10:11 + 11:25 + 14:6 + 15:1 (the seven Johannine I-AM sayings) is therefore self-identification with the Burning-Bush God. Tewahedo Christological-catechesis cites Ex 3:14 + Jn 8:58 + the seven I-AM sayings as the single-Person-of-the-Word-incarnate confession.

✧ Variant. YHWH and the LXX. The four Hebrew letters yod-heh-vav-heh (יהוה) are the personal divine name. By the post-exilic period it was no longer pronounced aloud; readers substituted Adonai (“my Lord”). The LXX consistently translates with Kyrios (“Lord”), a convention that flowed into the New Testament and English Bibles (which usually print “the LORD” in small caps for YHWH). This translation choice flattens the distinction between the proper name YHWH and the title Adon in the underlying Hebrew.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Moses' hand made leprous in the bosom and then restored is, for Ephrem, the sign of the Incarnation given before the fact: humanity has become diseased in its hidden parts, and the Lord places it within his own bosom to bring it forth healed. The same hand that becomes leprous becomes healing for the leprous — a foreshadowing of the Word's assumption of the very flesh he will cleanse.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Water turned to blood at Moses' word is the sign of judgment; water turned to wine at Cana is the sign of joy. Ephrem reads the two miracles as a single canonical inclusio: the first prophet inverts the river to bring judgment on Egypt; the true Lord inverts the water-pots to bring gladness to the wedding. The Word who turned the Nile to blood for accusation turns the jars of purification into the wine of the new covenant.

⌘ Hebrew. K’vad-peh u-k’vad-lashon (כְבַד־פֶּה וּכְבַד לָשׁוֹן) — “heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue.” Two parallel idioms, neither a precise medical description. Ancient and medieval readers proposed everything from a stutter to a literal speech impediment to mere humility; the Hebrew is best taken as a self-deprecating idiom for being ill-suited to public speech. Aaron is given as Moses’ spokesman (4:14–16), and Moses’ own oratory in Deuteronomy seems to take place without difficulty.

◇ Note. Whose hand hardens Pharaoh’s heart? The book uses three distinct verbs (chazaq, kashah, kaved) and distributes the agency in a striking pattern: in chapters 7–9 Pharaoh hardens his own heart (or his heart simply “becomes hard”); only from chapter 10 onward does God explicitly do the hardening. Many readers (e.g. Origen, Maimonides, modern commentators like Childs) take the sequence to mean that judicial hardening confirms a will already fixed — God ratifies a choice Pharaoh has already made repeatedly.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

The hostile encounter at the lodging-place, where the Lord seems to seek Moses' life, Ephrem reads as a covenant-rupture answered by covenant-restoration: it is the failure to circumcise Moses' son that opens the breach, and Zipporah's prompt circumcision that closes it. The Tewahedo reading harmonizes the canonical witness with Jub 48:1-2, which names Mastema as the immediate agent; the divine permission and the demonic accusation work together to vindicate the covenant.

◇ Note. The most obscure passage in Exodus. Verses 24–26 are notoriously cryptic: God “seeks to kill” someone (Moses? his son?), Zipporah circumcises the boy and touches “his feet” (a Hebrew euphemism for genitals), and pronounces a phrase usually translated chatan damim, “bridegroom of blood.” Theories range from Moses’ failure to circumcise his own son, to a Midianite marriage rite the narrator has only partly preserved, to a textual fragment from a now-lost source. There is no scholarly consensus.

⌘ Hebrew. El Shaddai (אֵל שַׁדַּי) and the divine names. The verse claims the patriarchs knew God only as El Shaddai, not by the name YHWH — yet Genesis uses YHWH freely on Abraham’s lips. This tension is one of the foundational data-points for the Documentary Hypothesis, where the verse is read as the Priestly source’s claim that the divine name was first revealed at the Exodus. The etymology of Shaddai is itself disputed: from shadad (“to overpower”), from shad (“breast,” a fertility-god connection), or from Akkadian šadû (“mountain”).

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.19 (c. 350 AD)

'And the Lord said unto Moses, See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet' — Athanasius marks dedōka se theon tō Pharaō (I have given thee as a god to Pharaoh) as the METHODOLOGICAL-KEY for the gods-by-participation vs theotēs-by-nature distinction. Moses is called 'god' by ECONOMIC-COMMUNICATION (his role-as-divine-mediator to Pharaoh) and by DIVINE-GRACIOUS-GRANT, not by nature. The Word, by contrast, is God by-nature (kata physin), not by-grace (kata charin); is-eternally-God, not-made-god. Athanasius pairs Exo 7:1 with Psa 82:6 ('I have said, Ye are gods'; cf. Jn 10:34) as the canonical-theōsis-by-grace pair, contrasting both with the Son's-deity-by-essence. Crucial anti-Arian hermeneutical-grid.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

Aaron's rod swallowing the rods-turned-serpents of the magicians is, for Ephrem, an early figure of the Crucified Christ swallowing the dragon: the wood that becomes a serpent becomes a devouring serpent, and the devouring is itself the salvation. The Cross — wood that becomes the throne of the Serpent-conqueror — accomplishes in reality what the rod accomplished in type.

◇ Note. Egyptian magicians. Egyptian wisdom literature actively cultivated reputations for snake-charming and staff-tricks; turning a staff into a serpent is attested in Pharaonic temple rites. The narrative grants the magicians initial parity (they replicate the first three signs) before the contest decisively breaks open. Later Jewish tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, 2 Tim 3:8) names two of them Jannes and Jambres.

⌘ Hebrew. Etzba Elohim (אֶצְבַּע אֱלֹהִים) — “finger of God.” The Egyptian magicians’ confession is the first occurrence of an idiom that recurs at Sinai — the tablets of the Decalogue are written with the finger of God (Exod 31:18, Deut 9:10). The phrase implies a small, deliberate divine action — not the full “hand” of judgment but a measured sign. Jesus picks up the same idiom in Luke 11:20.

⌘ Hebrew. Pesach (פֶּסַח) — “passover” or “protective limping.” The verb pasach appears only in this and a handful of related passages. Traditional reading: God “passed over” the Hebrew houses. Recent semitic comparison (Akkadian pasāhu, “to placate”) and Isaiah 31:5’s parallel of YHWH “hovering / protecting” suggest the verb may originally have meant a protective stance — God stood guard over the doorways rather than skipping them. The Hebrew bears both senses.

⌘ Hebrew. Erev rav (עֵרֶב רַב) — “great mixture.” The phrase signals that the group leaving Egypt was not ethnically uniform: foreigners, slaves, and Egyptians sympathetic to the Hebrew cause joined the exodus. Later rabbinic tradition often blamed this group for the golden-calf episode and other rebellions; the text itself draws no such conclusion. The note is significant for understanding Israelite identity from the start as porous and adoptive.

✧ Variant. 430 years (MT) vs. 430 in Egypt and Canaan combined (LXX, Samaritan). The Masoretic Text says Israel sojourned in Egypt 430 years; the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch read “in Egypt and in the land of Canaan” — splitting the period across the patriarchal era and the Egyptian sojourn. Paul’s 430-year figure in Galatians 3:17 follows the LXX/Samaritan reading. Genesis 15:13 had said 400 years; the genealogies in Exodus 6 list only four generations from Levi to Moses, fitting better with the shorter LXX figure.

⌘ Hebrew. Chamushim (חֲמוּשִׁים) — “armed,” “in fives,” or “marshalled.” The word is a four-way pun in Hebrew. Its root chamesh (“five”) can yield: armed (with five weapons or five soldiers abreast); in groups of fifty (a tactical fifth); only one fifth (i.e. the small remnant willing to leave); or simply organized in ranks. Translators must pick one; ancient versions chose differently (LXX pemptē genea, “in the fifth generation”).

◇ Note. The pillar. A single pillar — cloud by day, fire by night — accompanies Israel as far as Sinai and (by 40:36–38) settles over the tabernacle. The motif fuses two ancient Near Eastern theophany images: the storm-cloud chariot of Baal/Marduk traditions and the temple-fire of cult presence. Within Exodus, it is the visible sign that the divine name now travels with this people.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

Moses stretches out the rod over the sea, and Ephrem hears in the gesture the shape of the Cross extended over the waters of baptism. The rod that splits the sea is the same wood that, in the new dispensation, splits the waters of death so that the baptized may walk through on dry ground. Tewahedo reads the Red Sea and the baptismal font as a single canonical passageway.

⌘ Hebrew. Yam suf (יַם־סוּף) — “Sea of Reeds.” The Hebrew name does not say “Red Sea”; it says literally “Reed-sea.” The LXX rendered it erythra thalassa (“Red Sea”) — possibly because by the third century BCE the term had drifted to denote the larger Red Sea body, or possibly through a separate naming tradition. Geographically, candidate locations range from a marshy lake on the eastern Nile delta to the Gulf of Suez or Aqaba; the text’s precise location is debated, but “Reed-sea” fits a freshwater marsh better than the open salt sea.

◇ Note. The Song of the Sea. Often considered one of the oldest passages in the Hebrew Bible (along with Judges 5 and Numbers 23–24). Linguistic features — archaic suffixes, rare vocabulary, parallelism without later prose connectives — point to genuinely early Hebrew, perhaps 13th–12th century BCE. If so, the song may be older than the surrounding prose narrative that frames it.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'I will sing unto the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously' — the first canonical hymn of victory, sung on the shore of the sea by the redeemed. Ephrem treats Ex 15:1 as the prototype of all Pascal hymnody: every Easter song of the Church is a continuation of Moses' shore-song. Tewahedo mäzmur-tradition recognizes the Song of Moses among its earliest canonical warrants for hymnic praise after deliverance.

⌘ Hebrew. Mi kamokha ba-elim YHWH (מִי־כָמֹכָה בָּאֵלִם יְהוָה). The Hebrew literally asks: “Who is like you among the gods, O YHWH?” The construction implies the existence of other elim (gods) — YHWH is incomparable but not (yet) the only one. This kind of comparative monotheism (technically monolatry: one god worshipped among many recognized) is widespread in early biblical poetry; full philosophical monotheism (“no other gods exist”) emerges more clearly in later prophets like Isaiah 40–55.

Called nevi’ah (“prophetess”) here — only the second woman to receive that title in Hebrew scripture (after the unnamed mother of Isaiah’s sons in Isa 8:3 chronologically, but Miriam’s use is older textually). ⌘ Hebrew. Segullah (סְגֻלָּה) — “treasured possession.” The word denotes a private treasure of a king — items personally owned, distinct from the property of the realm. ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage' — Ephrem reads the Pascal preface as the ground of every command that follows. The commandments are not arbitrary statutes but the rule-of-life of a delivered people; only the delivered are addressed by the Decalogue. Tewahedo catechesis preserves this priority of deliverance before commandment.

⌘ Hebrew. Shabbat (שַׁבָּת) — to cease. The verb shavat means simply to stop, not “to rest” in the sense of recovery. The Sabbath commandment in Deuteronomy 5 grounds the day in liberation from slavery; here in Exodus 20 it is grounded in creation (Gen 2:2–3). The two rationales coexist throughout Israelite tradition: the day is at once cosmic and political — a weekly enactment of being a free creature in a created world.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy' — Ephrem reads Sabbath-rest as the canonical sign that creation is given a goal beyond labour: the Sabbath foreshadows the eighth-day rest of the Resurrection. Tewahedo alone among the major communions preserves both observances together — Saturday-Sabbath retained from Sinai and Sunday-Lord's-Day added from the Resurrection — and reads Ex 20:8 as the canonical anchor of the double observance.

⌘ Hebrew. Lo tirtzach (לֹא תִרְצָח). The verb ratzach denotes unlawful, personal killing — what English calls murder — not all forms of killing. The Hebrew Bible elsewhere uses different verbs (harag, hemit) for warfare and judicial execution, both of which the Torah continues to permit. Older English translations (KJV “thou shalt not kill”) blur this distinction; modern translations almost universally restore it.

◇ Note. The firstborn. The Passover institution turns the death of the firstborn (Exod 12) into a permanent claim on Israel’s firstborn — redeemed by substitute offering (13:13) or, for the priestly tribe, by Levite substitution (Num 3:12). Luke 2:23 cites this verse describing the presentation of Jesus at the Temple. The redemption-of-firstborn ceremony (pidyon ha-ben) on the thirty-first day of life remains a Jewish practice descending directly from this text.

◇ Note. Manna theology. The wilderness manna (described botanically in Num 11:7–9) is read as a sustained miracle of divine provision contingent on daily trust. Wisdom of Solomon 16:20 turns it into "food of angels"; John 6 has Jesus identifying himself as the true manna ("I am the bread of life"). The double-portion-on-Friday rule (16:5) embeds the Sabbath into the very logistics of survival — divine provisioning that itself rests.

◇ Note. Jethro’s counsel. A non-Israelite priest of Midian gives Moses governance advice — and Moses takes it. The narrative is theologically generous: wisdom can come from outside the covenant community. The system Jethro proposes (chiefs of thousands, hundreds, fifties, tens) becomes the template for Israelite judicial administration. The Qumran community’s organizational documents (1QS) draw on this same passage for their hierarchical structure.

◇ Note. The first commandment. The Hebrew ‘al panai ("before/beside my face") admits two readings: monolatry (Yahweh alone among existing gods is to be worshipped) or strict monotheism (no other gods exist). Most modern scholarship reads early Israelite religion as monolatrous, with explicit monotheism crystallizing later (Isaiah 40–55). The Decalogue’s grammar fits the monolatrous reading more naturally; the systematic monotheism becomes explicit in Deuteronomy and the prophets.

◇ Note. The alien protection laws. The motivation clause is unusual in ancient Near Eastern law: not a command from royal authority, but appeal to shared experience ("you were aliens in Egypt"). This formulation appears 36+ times in the Pentateuch — making protection of the foreigner one of the most repeated commandments in Torah. The same logic recurs in Deut 10:19 and Lev 19:33–34 ("love him as yourself"), where the foreigner becomes a paradigm-case for the love commandment.

⌘ Hebrew. ʼôwr (אוֹר). illumination or (concrete) luminary (in every sense, including lightning, happiness, etc.). [Reviewer: extend this with context, theological reading, and any cross-canon resonance before promoting.]

⌘ Hebrew. V’shakhanti b’tokham (וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹכָם). The verb shakhan ("dwell, tabernacle") generates the noun mishkan (tabernacle) and the later rabbinic shekhinah (the indwelling presence). John 1:14 ("the Word became flesh and dwelt — eskēnōsen, tabernacled — among us") deliberately echoes this verse via the LXX. The verse establishes the central theological claim of the second half of Exodus: God’s purpose in delivering Israel from Egypt is dwelling among them.

◇ Note. Moses’ Levite genealogy. The narrative opens Moses’ story without naming his parents — Amram and Jochebed are named only later (6:20). The deliberate anonymity heightens the sense that this child arrives without context, found rather than born into rank. The detail that both parents are Levites is theologically loaded: Moses comes from the tribe that will, by the end of Exodus, be set apart for sanctuary service.

⌘ Hebrew. ’Ehyeh asher ’ehyeh (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה). The most famous verbal puzzle in the Hebrew Bible. The verb hayah ("to be") is in the first-person imperfect, which can render as: "I am that I am," "I will be what I will be," "I am the one who is," "I cause to be what is." The LXX gives egō eimi ho ōn ("I am the One who is"), influencing all subsequent Greek-philosophical reading of God as Being itself. Maimonides took the Hebrew as denoting necessary existence; Ricoeur as fidelity-promise; Buber as presence ("I shall be present"). The form connects to the divine name YHWH (also from the root h-y-h).

◇ Note. The Bridegroom of Blood. One of the strangest passages in the Pentateuch. As Moses is en route to Egypt — having just been commissioned — God attacks him at a night encampment. Zipporah saves him by circumcising her son and touching Moses’s feet with the blood, declaring "a bridegroom of blood you are to me." The episode foreshadows Passover: blood of circumcision saves Moses, blood of the lamb saves Israel.

◇ Note. Pesaḥ (פֶּסַח). The verb pasaḥ, source of the festival name, occurs in v.13 ("I will pass over") and probably means "to limp," "to skip," or "to spare." The festival meal is to be eaten standing, dressed for travel — eternalizing the urgency of the Exodus night. The Christian Eucharist takes its institution from this meal (Mark 14:12–25). The Ethiopian Tewahedo Church preserves a strong Passover-Eucharist link in its liturgy.

◇ Note. Tefillin. Together with Deut 6:8 and 11:18, this verse is the basis for the Jewish practice of binding scriptural texts in small leather cases on the arm and head. The literal interpretation became normative; the Karaites later argued for a metaphorical reading. The phrase "a memorial between your eyes" gives the head-tefillin its place; "a sign on your hand" gives the arm-tefillin its place. Pharisaic-rabbinic literalism here vs. spiritualizing readings represents one of the deepest interpretive divergences in Second Temple Judaism.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Israel passes through the sea on dry ground with the waters as a wall on either hand. Paul reads this as 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea' (1 Cor 10:2); Ephrem follows Paul and reads Ex 14:22 as the founding scriptural figure of Christian baptism. Tewahedo carries this as the principal OT type of its baptismal liturgy: the people pass through the waters and emerge a people.

◇ Note. The Sea of Reeds. The Hebrew yam suf is traditionally translated "Red Sea" via the LXX, but "Reed Sea" is closer to the Hebrew. Likely refers to a marshy lake region in the eastern Nile delta. The miracle is described differently in different sources within the chapter: a strong east wind drying the sea (14:21 — naturalistic), water as walls (14:22 — supernatural). Both readings are kept side by side in the canonical text.

◇ Note. The Song of the Sea. Exodus 15 is one of the oldest poetic strata of the Hebrew Bible (alongside Judges 5, the Song of Deborah). Its archaic Hebrew, parallelism, and triumphal celebration of God-as-warrior preserves a martial theology that later prophetic and wisdom traditions will both honor and complicate. The Ethiopian Tewahedo liturgy still incorporates this song. The image of God as warrior is uncomfortable for many modern readers; the Bible itself wrestles with it (cf. Isa 2:4, the swords-into-plowshares).

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

The rock struck by Moses' rod pours out water for the thirsty people, and Ephrem joins Paul (1 Cor 10:4) in reading the rock as Christ. The striking is the Crucifixion; the water is the Spirit and the eucharistic stream (Jn 19:34 — blood and water from the pierced side). Tewahedo treats Ex 17:6 and Jn 19:34 as a single canonical disclosure of the smitten Christ releasing the rivers of living water.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

When Moses lifted up his hands Israel prevailed against Amalek; when he let them down Amalek prevailed. Ephrem reads the cruciform posture as the secret of the victory: Moses' arms outstretched are the Cross fore-figured, and the war is won not by the sword in the valley but by the cross-shape on the hill. Tewahedo carries this as the canonical OT type of Christian intercessory prayer in the cross-posture.

◇ Note. The lifted hands. Moses’s upraised arms — held up by Aaron and Hur — became one of early Christianity’s most-cited typologies of the Cross (already in the Epistle of Barnabas 12; later in Justin, Tertullian, Augustine). The Ethiopian Tewahedo iconographic tradition preserves the same reading. Independent of the typology, the narrative is clear: the battle’s fortunes follow the prayer-posture, not the military skill.

◇ Note. Mamleket kohanim (מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים). The corporate priesthood of Israel — every member a priest before the nations. 1 Peter 2:9 applies the same phrase to the Church. The democratization of priesthood is one of Israel’s distinctive contributions to ancient religious thought; in surrounding ANE cultures, priesthood was a royal-administrative class. Israel inverts: the whole people is mediator.

◇ Note. The First Commandment. "Before me" (‘al panay) more literally "in my presence" or "to my face." Some scholars distinguish monolatry (worshipping one God while granting others exist) from monotheism (denying others exist) — and read this commandment as monolatry, with monotheism developing later (Deut 4:35, Isa 44:6). The classical Jewish and Christian reading, however, takes the commandment as already implicitly monotheistic.

◇ Note. The covenant meal. One of the most extraordinary passages in scripture: the seventy elders "see God" and eat with him on the mountain. The text immediately notes God did not lay a hand on them — i.e., they survived the encounter. The pavement of sapphire under God’s feet later becomes a stock image in apocalyptic literature (Ezek 1:26). The communal meal in God’s presence prefigures Eucharistic theology.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them' — Ephrem reads this verse as the canonical warrant for every consecrated dwelling-place of God: the tabernacle prefigures the Incarnation ('the Word was made flesh and tabernacled among us,' Jn 1:14), and the Incarnation prefigures the Church. Tewahedo cites Ex 25:8 as the principal canonical anchor of its tabot tradition — the Ark-as-sanctuary at the center of every Tewahedo church.

⌘ Hebrew. Shakanti (שָׁכַנְתִּי) — "I will dwell." The verb gives us mishkan, "tabernacle" (the dwelling), and later Shekhinah — the rabbinic/mystical term for God’s indwelling presence. John 1:14 echoes this when he says the Logos "tabernacled (eskēnōsen) among us" — the Greek echoes the same root. The whole tabernacle theology of Exodus is reread Christologically through this single verb.

◇ Note. Pharaoh’s question. Pharaoh’s "Who is Yahweh?" is the theological problem the rest of the book is going to answer. The Egyptian king’s question is asked from a polytheistic premise — he assumes Yahweh is one tribal deity among many — and the entire plague sequence is structured as an extended answer: Yahweh is the one whose power demonstrably surpasses every Egyptian deity (Hapi the Nile-god in plague 1, Heqet the frog-goddess in plague 2, etc.; cf. 12:12, "I will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt"). The narrative is theologically self-conscious: the question Pharaoh asks ironically becomes the structuring rhetorical question of the next ten chapters. By 9:27 Pharaoh confesses "Yahweh is righteous"; by 12:31 he commands the exodus he initially refused. The narrative architecture is deliberately catechetical — the king who did not know Yahweh learns through plague, and the reader learns alongside him.

◇ Note. The Israelite foremen’s complaint. The Israelite foremen, beaten by Pharaoh’s slave-drivers because the people cannot meet the increased brick-quota, turn on Moses and Aaron with bitter accusation: their advocacy has made things worse. The episode is the first of many in which Israel itself becomes Moses’ opposition — a pattern that will run through the wilderness narratives and become the deuteronomistic theme of "stiff-necked" Israel. The verse is also psychologically realistic about how oppression frequently turns the oppressed against their advocates rather than the oppressors: when liberation produces immediate worsening before improvement, the advocates become the visible cause of the suffering. The narrative refuses to romanticize the people Moses is leading; it consistently shows them as ungrateful, frightened, and shortsighted. The honesty is theologically programmatic — Yahweh does not redeem Israel because Israel deserves redemption but because Yahweh has made covenant promises that bind even when the recipients are unworthy.

◇ Note. The Egyptian magicians. Pharaoh’s court magicians replicate the first plagues with their latim ("secret arts"), then fail at the gnats (8:18) and confess "this is the finger of God." Egyptian magical literature (the Demotic Magical Papyri, Coffin Texts) confirms the historical reality of the priestly-magical class the text portrays. Jewish tradition names two of them, Yannes and Yambres (cited in 2 Tim 3:8), expanding the narrative through pseudepigraphic literature.

◇ Note. The plague-distinction principle. Beginning here (in plague 5, the cattle-pestilence) and intensifying through plagues 6–10, the narrative consistently distinguishes Egyptian from Israelite suffering: only Egyptian livestock die, only Egypt experiences darkness (10:23), only Egyptian firstborn perish (12:29–30). The principle — Yahweh making "a distinction" (palah, 11:7) between Egyptian and Israelite — frames the exodus as judicial-discriminating action rather than indiscriminate plague. Theologically it answers the question why Israelites were not affected: not because they were geographically separate (Goshen is not far from Egyptian population centers) but because Yahweh’s judgment is targeted. The Passover ritual of ch 12 will operationalize the same principle at the family level: blood on the doorpost makes the household a discriminated zone. The exodus narrative’s entire theological logic — judgment against Egypt, deliverance for Israel — depends on this principle of discriminating divine action.

◇ Note. "For this purpose I have raised you up." The verse is one of the OT’s most theologically charged formulations of divine sovereignty over human history: Pharaoh’s very existence as Egyptian king is portrayed as instrumental to Yahweh’s revelation. Paul cites this verse explicitly at Rom 9:17 in his sustained meditation on divine election, sovereignty, and human responsibility — making it one of the foundational texts for the entire Christian theological tradition on predestination. Augustine, Calvin, and Aquinas all engage Rom 9 (and through it this verse) at length; Pelagius, Erasmus, and Arminius read it differently. The OT verse itself is deliberately vivid — Yahweh has not just permitted Pharaoh’s recalcitrance but has positioned the king "for this purpose." The same divine sovereignty over an opposing king’s heart will recur in Cyrus (Isa 45:1, "Yahweh’s anointed") and even Nebuchadnezzar (Jer 25:9, "my servant"). The verse encodes one of the OT’s most uncompromising formulations of the deity’s control over human political action.

◇ Note. The locust plague. Locusts (Heb. arbeh) were the most feared agricultural disaster in the ANE — a single swarm could consume the food supply of a regional population. Egyptian sources confirm the destructive potential: the Famine Stela of the Ptolemaic era retrojects locust catastrophes onto Djoser’s reign as the worst-imaginable catastrophe; Ugaritic and Mesopotamian texts treat locust swarms as divine punishment by default. The plague’s theological significance: it strikes Egypt’s remaining agriculture after the hail of plague 7, depriving Pharaoh’s court of food — the chapter is the OT’s clearest articulation of plagues working in cumulative economic logic. Joel 1–2 takes the locust plague as the prophetic image of Yahweh’s eschatological "Day of the Lord," developing the Exodus pattern into apocalyptic vocabulary. The verse’s superlative formula ("never were there such locusts before, nor shall there be again") is part of the chapter’s deliberate intensification — each plague exceeds the last.

◇ Note. The ninth plague. The three days of palpable darkness — Hebrew "darkness which may be felt" (yamesh ḥoshekh) — is the most cosmically pointed of the plagues: it directly attacks Ra, the Egyptian sun-god and supreme deity of the New Kingdom pantheon. The Egyptian theology of kingship rested on the Pharaoh’s identification with Ra’s son and the Pharaoh’s preservation of the cosmic order against the encroaching darkness. This plague reverses that order: darkness reigns over Egypt while the Israelites in Goshen have light (10:23). The plague functions as the immediate prelude to the climactic plague of the firstborn — Egyptian theology’s sun-god having been demonstrably overcome, the Pharaoh’s own status as Ra’s son will be the next target. The Wisdom of Solomon (17:2–18:4) develops the verse into an elaborate meditation on the spiritual darkness of Egypt’s injustice contrasted with the light of Israel’s deliverance. The plague is the theological hinge of the cycle.

◇ Note. The firstborn judgment. The threatened final plague targets the firstborn male of every Egyptian household — from Pharaoh’s royal heir to the firstborn of household servants, plus the firstborn of livestock. The targeting is theologically precise: "Israel is my firstborn son" (4:22), and Pharaoh’s refusal to release Yahweh’s firstborn is now answered by the death of Egypt’s firstborns. The principle — measure for measure (middah k’neged middah in later rabbinic vocabulary) — is one of the OT’s recurrent theological-judicial frameworks. The Passover ritual of ch 12 functions as the Israelite firstborn’s ransom: blood on the doorpost substitutes for the firstborn’s death, grounding the OT theology of substitutionary atonement that later Christian thought (especially Heb 9–10) develops Christologically. The verse is the structural pivot of the entire exodus narrative — the plague that Pharaoh cannot withstand, that produces the immediate release.

◇ Note. The silence of the dogs. The detail — not a single dog will growl during the firstborn plague — registers the absolute supernatural quiet that will accompany the night of the angel of death’s passage through Egypt. The image is precise and chilling: in any normal night-event of mass death, dogs across the city would bark in chorus; the silence is the signature of divinely calibrated judgment. Egyptian dogs were associated with Anubis, the jackal-headed god of the dead — the silent dogs may be a small, pointed signal that Anubis himself has been overcome, that the Egyptian death-pantheon is paralyzed during the very night Yahweh visits Egypt with death. The detail also belongs to the chapter’s broader pattern of distinguishing Israel from Egypt: Israel’s livestock and people will be silent and unaffected, only Egypt will hear the cry of universal lamentation (12:30, "a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead"). The contrast of cosmic noise against absolute silence is the chapter’s most striking literary effect.

◇ Note. The Song of the Sea. One of the oldest preserved poems in Hebrew, datable on linguistic grounds to the late second millennium BCE — quite possibly older than the prose narrative that introduces it. Its archaic forms (yqtl tense usage, enclitic mem, infrequent definite article) are diagnostic. The song closes with Yahweh enthroned forever (15:18) — possibly the earliest royal-cosmic-kingship statement in the Bible. The Mishnah (Pesachim 10) lists this song as part of the Hallel sung at Passover.

◇ Note. The pierced-ear ceremony. The provision concerns the Hebrew slave whose six-year term has ended (cf. 21:2) but who chooses, out of love for his master’s family, to remain a permanent member of the household: he is brought to "God" (the household tribunal, or the local sanctuary) and his ear is pierced against the doorpost as a permanent mark. The ceremony combines several theological registers: the doorway as threshold of household identity (cf. 12:7, the Passover blood on doorposts), the ear as the organ of obedience (cf. Pss 40:6–8, "ears you have dug for me," cited Christologically at Heb 10:5–7), and the irreversible mark of permanent commitment. Paul’s self-designation as "slave of Christ Jesus" (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1) draws on the same conceptual world — the freed person who chooses lifelong service. The Hebrew slave-law generally is one of the OT’s remarkable institutions: a worker is enslaved for at most six years, with the seventh year as automatic release (21:2) — far more humane than most ANE slave-codes.

◇ Note. Lex talionis at Sinai. The first occurrence of the talion formula in the Pentateuch (also Lev 24:20, Deut 19:21). In its ANE legal context, the formula functions as a limit on retaliation: punishment must be proportional, never excessive. Hammurabi §§196–197 includes literal mutilations as the realized form; Hebrew rabbinic interpretation (Mekhilta on Exodus 21, b. Bava Kamma 83b–84a) understood the formula from the start as referring to monetary compensation calibrated to lost function rather than literal mutilation. Whether the rabbinic reading reflects original intent or interpretive softening is debated; literal mutilation is rare in actual Jewish legal practice. Jesus’ "you have heard it said… but I say to you" (Matt 5:38–39) does not abolish the proportionality limit but transcends it: refuse retaliation entirely. The verse is one of the most consistently misunderstood OT texts in popular reception — read as license for revenge when the original purpose was the opposite.

◇ Note. The alien-protection clause. One of the OT’s most-repeated commands, occurring in slightly varying forms more than thirty times across the Pentateuch and prophets (cf. Lev 19:33–34, Deut 10:19, 24:14–22, Jer 7:6, Zech 7:10, Mal 3:5). The grounding rationale here is experiential: "you know the heart of an alien, since you were aliens in the land of Egypt." The provision uses Israel’s own historical trauma as the moral foundation for treatment of immigrants — Israel knows what it feels like to be a foreigner mistreated, and that knowledge becomes covenantal obligation. The principle is one of the OT’s clearest examples of empathy-based ethics: the experience of suffering is to be converted into the policy of refusing to inflict that same suffering on others. The contemporary political resonance is sharp; the provision has been a major reference point in modern Jewish and Christian advocacy for refugee and immigrant protection. Few OT verses have so direct an application across such a long stretch of legal-political history.

◇ Note. The first occurrence of the kid-in-milk prohibition. The verse appears three times in the Pentateuch (here, 34:26, Deut 14:21) — a triple attestation that, in rabbinic interpretation (b. Hullin 113b), generates the threefold separation of meat from milk in kashrut: not cooking together, not eating together, not benefiting from the mixture. The literal practice the verse forbids is documented in 14th-century-BCE Ugaritic ritual texts (KTU 1.23, the "Birth of the Gracious Gods"), where boiling a kid in milk appears as a Canaanite ritual gesture — making the verse a pointed prohibition of a specific known pagan rite. The rabbinic generalization is therefore an interpretive expansion well beyond the literal sense, but the literal sense itself is precisely calibrated: avoid the cultic practice of the surrounding peoples. The verse is one of the OT’s most striking examples of how a single ritual prohibition can generate an entire dietary tradition.

◇ Note. The covenant formula. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest articulations of the so-called "covenant formula" — the bilateral commitment "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" (cf. Lev 26:12, Jer 7:23, 11:4, 24:7, 30:22, 31:33, Ezek 11:20, 36:28, 37:23, 27, Zech 8:8). The formula compresses the entire substance of covenantal relationship into a single bidirectional clause: divine self-commitment to be Israel’s God, Israel’s self-commitment to be Yahweh’s people. The formula’s eschatological development at Rev 21:3 ("the dwelling of God is with men, and they will be his people") makes it one of the canonical bookends of biblical theology — appearing here at Israel’s formation and recurring at the consummation of all things. The chapter places the formula within Yahweh’s response to Israel’s discouragement (cf. 5:21–6:1) — covenant identity is asserted precisely when the covenant partners cannot yet feel it.

◇ Note. The "you shall know" refrain. The phrase "you shall know that I am Yahweh" (Hebrew vidatem ki ani Adonai) recurs as the structuring rhetorical refrain of the plague narratives (cf. 7:5, 8:10, 8:22, 9:14, 9:29, 10:2, 14:4, 14:18) and becomes one of Ezekiel’s most distinctive formulas — the prophet uses it more than 70 times across his book. Its theological function is precise: the plagues are not just punishment but pedagogy, delivering knowledge of Yahweh to Egyptians, Israelites, and the surrounding nations. The verse establishes the principle that divine action is inherently revelatory — Yahweh acts in history not just to accomplish ends but to make himself known. The principle becomes one of the load-bearing premises of OT theology, with prophetic-historical action consistently framed as divine self-disclosure rather than as bare power-assertion. The verse is theologically the most concentrated single line in plague 1.

◇ Note. The frog plague. Heqet, the Egyptian frog-headed goddess, was associated with childbirth and fertility — the swarming frogs of plague 2 directly target an Egyptian deity. The plague’s theological precision matches the pattern of the cycle: each plague disables a specific Egyptian deity (Hapi the Nile-god in plague 1, Heqet here, Geb the earth-god in plague 3, Khepri the scarab-god in plague 4, etc.). The plague is also unique in that Pharaoh’s magicians can replicate it (8:7) but cannot stop it — they can multiply frogs but cannot remove them. The detail is psychologically devastating: the magicians’ "success" only worsens the catastrophe. Ps 78:45 and 105:30 commemorate the plague specifically. The chapter’s opening verses also encode a wordplay: the Hebrew "frog" (tzefarde‘a) appears in the singular collectively (8:6, "the frog covered the land of Egypt"), giving the impression of one massive amphibian-blanket rather than discrete creatures.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'I will rain bread from heaven for you' — the manna of the wilderness is for Ephrem the direct prophetic anchor of Jn 6: 'I am the bread which came down from heaven.' The wilderness bread sustains the body for a day; the Eucharist sustains the soul for eternity. Tewahedo Anaphora cites Ex 16:4 and Jn 6 together as the OT-NT diptych of the eucharistic gift.

⌘ Hebrew. Man hu (מָן הוּא). The Israelites’ question on first seeing the desert food — "What is it?" (man hu) — becomes the food’s permanent name: man, "manna." The text is doing folk-etymology, but with theological intent: the food’s name encodes Israel’s ignorance about it. The Hebrew preserves the puzzlement: this is not bread, not flesh, not anything Israel has a vocabulary for. The substance is described botanically (16:31, "like coriander seed, white, with the taste of wafers made with honey") but never identified — which is the point. Manna is engineered to be theologically useful in its physical inexplicability. Jesus’ "I am the bread of life" discourse in John 6 (especially 6:31–58) takes this verse as central type — the bread that comes down from heaven, that supplies inexplicably, becomes Christological figure. Heb 9:4 records that a jar of manna was preserved inside the ark as one of three sacred memorials (with the rod and the tablets). The verse is the OT root of one of the most theologically productive food-images in biblical tradition.

◇ Note. The rock at Horeb. The first water-from-the-rock episode (cf. the second at Num 20:8–13, where Moses’ disobedience costs him the land). Paul cites this rock at 1 Cor 10:4 in one of the NT’s most striking typological readings: "they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ." The rabbinic tradition Paul draws on (cf. Tosefta Sukkah 3:11) imagines the rock literally accompanying Israel through the wilderness as a perpetual water-source; Paul takes the tradition and Christologizes it. The chapter’s placement of the episode at "Horeb" (the alternate name for Sinai) is geographically suggestive — the very mountain of covenant-giving will turn out to be the site of water-from-rock. The episode also generates a place-name pun: "Massah" (testing) and "Meribah" (quarreling), 17:7 — Israel’s wilderness skepticism materialized as toponym. The verse opens one of the OT’s richest typological clusters in the entire Pentateuch.

◇ Note. The blasphemy-and-ruler clause. The verse couples two prohibitions: cursing God and cursing a ruler (Hebrew nasi, "leader, prince"). The pairing assumes a theology of derivative authority — the ruler’s legitimacy participates in divine authority, and cursing the ruler is therefore cognate with cursing God. Paul cites this verse at Acts 23:5 (apologizing to the high priest Ananias whom Paul has rebuked: "I did not know, brothers, that he was high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people’"). The passage’s NT use is theologically significant: Paul, even when correctly accusing the high priest of judicial corruption, treats the verse as binding on his own speech. The verse’s narrower legal effect in OT context concerns courtroom speech — false accusation, public cursing, defamatory speech against community leaders — and connects to the broader OT prohibitions on perjury and false witness. The chapter is one of the OT’s clearest treatments of speech-acts as legally consequential.

◇ Note. The blood of the covenant. Moses splashes half the sacrificial blood on the altar and half on the people, formally inaugurating the Sinai covenant. The phrase "the blood of the covenant" (Hebrew dam ha-b’rit) becomes one of the most theologically charged in scripture: Jesus deliberately echoes it at the Last Supper ("this is my blood of the covenant," Matt 26:28, Mark 14:24, Luke 22:20, 1 Cor 11:25), framing the eucharist as the new analog to the Sinai blood-rite. Heb 9:18–22 makes the parallel explicit: the OT covenant required blood, the new covenant is similarly inaugurated with blood. The detail of the chapter — Moses sprinkling half on the altar (Yahweh’s side) and half on the people (the human partners) — encodes a theology of covenantal binding through shared substance. Few OT rituals have so directly shaped subsequent Christian sacramental theology and liturgical language. The chapter is the institutional and theological foundation of every later "blood of the covenant" formulation in the canon.

'I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God' — Ephrem hears in this verse the completion of the Abrahamic-Isaac-Jacob promise: the patriarchal seed becomes a peoplehood under a single covenanted Name. ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Pharaoh's host drowned in the very waters through which Israel walks dry is, for Ephrem, the canonical anti-type of baptism: what saves the believer destroys the pursuer. The devil and the powers of the old age are drowned in the font as Pharaoh was drowned in the sea. Tewahedo reads the renunciation of Satan in its baptismal rite as the liturgical correlate of the Red-Sea drowning.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

The Lord shows Moses a tree, and the tree cast into the bitter waters of Marah makes them sweet. Ephrem reads the wood as the Cross before its time: what sweetens the waters of the world is the wood of the Cross cast into them. Tewahedo Holy-Week catechesis cites Ex 15:25 as one of its principal OT cross-typology anchors.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

When Israel sees the manna they say 'man hu' — 'what is it?' — and the question itself becomes the name. Ephrem hears in this the canonical instinct that the heavenly food cannot be named by its likeness to anything earthly; the name is a confession of mystery. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites this as the OT antecedent of its own anaphoral language of 'mystery,' 'gift,' and 'medicine of life.'

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Sinai wrapped in fire and smoke is, for Ephrem, the OT diptych of Pentecost: there the fire descends on a mountain and the people may not come near; here the fire descends on heads and tongues so that the people themselves become the mountain. Tewahedo reads Ex 19:18 and Acts 2 as the before-and-after of the divine fire — the same fire that thundered now rests on the believer without consuming.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Two cherubim of gold beaten out of one piece, their wings stretched over the mercy seat, are for Ephrem the canonical sign that the divine throne rests over a place of propitiation, not over a tribunal alone. The mercy seat between the wings is the OT type of the Cross where mercy meets the Law. Tewahedo iconography preserves the cherub-flanked tabot in every sanctuary.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

The pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, leading Israel through the wilderness, is for Ephrem the canonical figure of Christ's two natures: the cloud that veils the fire is the humanity that veils the divinity, yet the veiling does not extinguish the radiance. Tewahedo reads the pillar as the first systematic OT diptych of the Incarnation.

◇ Note. The Jethro reform. The verse codifies one of the OT’s most institutionally consequential reorganizations: Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, a Midianite priest (and therefore a non-Israelite), advises Moses to delegate ordinary judicial cases to a hierarchical structure of judges over 1,000s, 100s, 50s, and 10s — keeping only the difficult cases for himself. The pattern recurs in Israelite military and judicial organization through the rest of the OT (Deut 1:15, 1 Sam 22:7, 2 Kgs 1:9–14). The provision’s narrative significance is theological: the institutional design Yahweh’s people will use is brought into Israel by a Midianite outsider, and Yahweh’s people accept it. The chapter quietly acknowledges that wisdom from outside Israel can legitimately shape Israelite institutions — a stance importantly different from the conquest-rhetoric of separation that dominates other parts of the Pentateuch. Jethro’s blessing (18:10–12) is also unusual: a non-Israelite priest pronounces benedictions over Yahweh’s deeds and offers sacrifice with Aaron and the elders. The chapter is one of the OT’s most positive portraits of religious-cultural exchange.

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)
